environmentalPersistence: Low as free acid — rapidly neutralized; nitrate ion persists and contributes to eutrophication

morphologicalEffects.heightSuppression: Moderate — similar to sulfuric acid but slightly less soil pH impact
morphologicalEffects.leafCurl: Moderate — cuticle damage; slightly less structural damage than H₂SO₄
morphologicalEffects.necrosis: Strong — acid burn necrosis at contact points; slightly less than H₂SO₄
morphologicalEffects.rootGrowth: Moderately inhibited by soil acidification; nitrate excess also causes root tip damage
morphologicalEffects.newVsOldLeaves: Contact-exposed leaves affected immediately regardless of age

physiologyEffects.additionalNote: Nitrate at low doses is actually a nutrient — this is the key distinction from sulfuric acid for educational purposes

molecularEffects.oxidativeStress: Strong — nitric acid generates reactive nitrogen species (RNS) in addition to ROS

microbiomeEffects.diversityReduction: Strong — acidification and nitrate excess disrupt microbiome
microbiomeEffects.beneficialBacteriaEffect: Strongly suppressed — nitrogen-fixing bacteria especially sensitive

temporalDynamics.recoveryTime: Poor for contact damage; soil recovery possible with buffering

visualSimulation.colorChanges: Bleaching at contact → necrotic brown; interveinal chlorosis pattern
visualSimulation.damagePattern: Similar to sulfuric acid — interveinal necrosis/bleaching; slightly more irregular
visualSimulation.heatmapGlow: Moderate — nitrate and MDA signature; nitrosylated protein peak distinctive
visualSimulation.recoveryVisual: Minimal — contact damage permanent; new growth healthy if acid source removed

synergies.synergyNote: Real-world acid rain is always a mixture of both acids — HNO₃ and H₂SO₄ together create faster and more complete cuticle dissolution than either alone

educationalContext.realWorldSources: NOₓ emissions from vehicles and power plants → atmospheric oxidation to HNO₃; lightning (natural source)
educationalContext.agriculturalUse: Fertilizer production intermediate; dilute form used in pH adjustment
educationalContext.humanToxicity: High — strong oxidizing acid; severe burns; nitrous fumes highly toxic to lungs
educationalContext.climateLink: Vehicle and power plant NOₓ emissions directly linked to acid rain; reducing combustion reduces HNO₃ deposition
educationalContext.whyStudentsCare: The acid rain crisis taught a generation that air pollution crosses borders — acid from US power plants damaged Canadian forests. An early example of transboundary pollution.
educationalContext.realWorldIssue: Transboundary acid rain, vehicle emissions, forest and lake acidification

sources: Likens GE, Bormann FH (1974). Acid rain: a serious regional environmental problem. Science, 184(4142), 1176–1179.
